summary: A 1975 commentary on using procedure calls as a network protocol. It discusses issues in building distributed computing systems and the shortcomings of RFC 674. See also RFC 542 and RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 684 questions whether computers on a network should work together by calling procedures on one another. It argues that independent processes exchanging messages better reflect the way distributed systems operate.

questions: remote procedure call versus message passing
what is rfc 684's critique of pcp
subtitle: A critique of using procedure calls as the foundation for distributed systems.

tldr.problem: RFC 684 argues that the Procedure Call Protocol treats distributed computing too much like a single program controlled from one place.
tldr.mechanism: The author favors independent processes coordinating through requests, replies and communication paths, and lists issues with applying procedure calls across machines.
tldr.outcome: The commentary accepts PCP's use as the base for the National Software Works project but argues against making its philosophy a general network standard.

today: The unit records RFC 684's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It records a 1975 critique of the distributed-computing approach in RFC 674.

sections.title: A Commentary on the Procedure Call Protocol
sections.content:
Richard Schantz presents RFC 684 as a first step toward discussion of distributed-system design. It comments on the Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) described in RFC 674, focusing on the ideas behind the design rather than its implementation details.

The author does not object to using PCP as the base-level implementation vehicle for the National Software Works project. He objects to treating the PCP approach as a general-purpose standard for distributed computation.
sections.plainLanguage: This note critiques the basic design idea in PCP, rather than how a particular implementation works. The author wants to discuss whether the same approach should be used for other distributed systems.

sections.title: Requests and Messages Instead of Remote Calls
sections.content:
The authors question PCP's premise that procedure calling should be the starting point for multi-computer systems. In their view, that premise creates a central point of control, while network processes are better treated as independent entities that cooperate over communication paths.

They favor a request-and-reply model between processes. Local procedure calls are cheap, but remote procedure calls require substantial system work; interprocess communication provides a model that applies more uniformly to local and remote processes.
sections.plainLanguage: A local procedure call is much cheaper than asking a process on another computer to run a procedure. The authors prefer messages between processes because that model makes the network boundary clear.

sections.title: Problems the Authors Identify
sections.content:
The commentary lists concerns about failure recovery, modularity, process initialization, asynchronous work and communication paths. It argues that a controlling process can manipulate another process's environment without its active participation, while a procedure-call model is awkward for long-running producer-consumer activity or multiple replies to one request.

The authors also question whether PCP is too complex for short, periodic exchanges and small hosts, whether it supports persistent or priority work cleanly, and whether it is intended as an implementation tool or an application interface. They conclude that it does not adequately model the complexities and possibilities of network environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the model can make it harder to recover from failures, isolate components and handle work that continues asynchronously. They conclude that a general distributed system needs a model built around communication between independent processes.

references.text: The Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) document being criticized.
